{
  "findings": [
    {
      "file": "pkg/services/cleanup/cleanup.go",
      "line": 77,
      "severity": "high",
      "category": "perf",
      "title": "Cleanup interval changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute",
      "body": "The background cleanup ticker is reduced from time.Minute*10 to time.Minute*1. This makes every cleanup job (temp files, snapshots, dashboard versions, images, annotations, invites, short URLs, query history) run ten times more frequently. The PR description only discusses the annotation deletion strategy, so this looks like a debugging/test leftover and can add significant database and filesystem load in production."
    },
    {
      "file": "pkg/services/annotations/annotationsimpl/xorm_store.go",
      "line": 534,
      "severity": "medium",
      "category": "bug",
      "title": "Normal cleanup progress is logged at Error level with full ID lists",
      "body": "CleanAnnotations and CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags log at Error level on every batch (lines 534, 537, 554, 557, 576, 579), including the full ids slice and a nil err. In normal operation this produces error-level log spam and can create very large log lines when batch sizes are large, which may trigger alerting or log-pipeline pressure. These should be Debug/Info and should not log entire ID lists."
    },
    {
      "file": "pkg/services/annotations/annotationsimpl/xorm_store.go",
      "line": 656,
      "severity": "medium",
      "category": "bug",
      "title": "Batch loop can exit early when fetched IDs were deleted concurrently",
      "body": "untilDoneOrCancelled stops when the callback returns affected == 0. After splitting SELECT and DELETE, a batch can fetch a non-empty set of IDs and then deleteByIDs can return 0 because another process deleted those rows between the two statements. More rows may still satisfy the cleanup condition, but the loop exits and cleanup is postponed. Completion should be based on whether the fetch returned an empty batch, or on fetched count, not solely on rows affected."
    },
    {
      "file": "pkg/services/annotations/annotationsimpl/xorm_store.go",
      "line": 615,
      "severity": "medium",
      "category": "bug",
      "title": "Single DELETE IN clause can exceed non-SQLite parameter limits",
      "body": "deleteByIDs builds one DELETE with one placeholder per fetched ID and only special-cases SQLite's 999 parameter limit. AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize is configurable, so on databases such as PostgreSQL/MySQL (around 65535 parameters) or MSSQL (around 2100 parameters) a large batch can generate too many bind parameters and make cleanup fail. The delete should be chunked or dialect parameter limits should be handled."
    },
    {
      "file": "pkg/services/annotations/annotationsimpl/xorm_store.go",
      "line": 611,
      "severity": "medium",
      "category": "perf",
      "title": "SQLite inline ID list is built with quadratic string concatenation",
      "body": "For SQLite, deleteByIDs builds the IN-list by repeatedly formatting the growing string with fmt.Sprintf. Each iteration copies the entire existing string, making the operation O(n^2) in the batch size. With the newly tested batch size of 32767, or larger configured values, this can cause unnecessary CPU and memory usage during cleanup. Use strings.Builder or strings.Join."
    }
  ]
}

findings.title: Cleanup interval changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute
findings.body: The background cleanup ticker is reduced from time.Minute*10 to time.Minute*1. This makes every cleanup job (temp files, snapshots, dashboard versions, images, annotations, invites, short URLs, query history) run ten times more frequently. The PR description only discusses the annotation deletion strategy, so this looks like a debugging/test leftover and can add significant database and filesystem load in production.

findings.title: Normal cleanup progress is logged at Error level with full ID lists
findings.body: CleanAnnotations and CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags log at Error level on every batch (lines 534, 537, 554, 557, 576, 579), including the full ids slice and a nil err. In normal operation this produces error-level log spam and can create very large log lines when batch sizes are large, which may trigger alerting or log-pipeline pressure. These should be Debug/Info and should not log entire ID lists.

findings.title: Batch loop can exit early when fetched IDs were deleted concurrently
findings.body: untilDoneOrCancelled stops when the callback returns affected == 0. After splitting SELECT and DELETE, a batch can fetch a non-empty set of IDs and then deleteByIDs can return 0 because another process deleted those rows between the two statements. More rows may still satisfy the cleanup condition, but the loop exits and cleanup is postponed. Completion should be based on whether the fetch returned an empty batch, or on fetched count, not solely on rows affected.

findings.title: Single DELETE IN clause can exceed non-SQLite parameter limits
findings.body: deleteByIDs builds one DELETE with one placeholder per fetched ID and only special-cases SQLite's 999 parameter limit. AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize is configurable, so on databases such as PostgreSQL/MySQL (around 65535 parameters) or MSSQL (around 2100 parameters) a large batch can generate too many bind parameters and make cleanup fail. The delete should be chunked or dialect parameter limits should be handled.

findings.title: SQLite inline ID list is built with quadratic string concatenation
findings.body: For SQLite, deleteByIDs builds the IN-list by repeatedly formatting the growing string with fmt.Sprintf. Each iteration copies the entire existing string, making the operation O(n^2) in the batch size. With the newly tested batch size of 32767, or larger configured values, this can cause unnecessary CPU and memory usage during cleanup. Use strings.Builder or strings.Join.
